transcript.en: Two students each asked forty classmates how long they spend on homework. One found fifty minutes and the other found sixty. Was one of them wrong? Today: why a sample never gives exactly the right answer, and how wrong it might be. The population is everyone we care about, say all eight hundred pupils. A sample is the group we actually ask. We use the sample to estimate something about the whole population. Pick forty pupils at random and you get one average. Pick another forty and you get a slightly different one. Neither student was wrong, because every random sample wobbles around the true value. We took twenty random samples from the school records and plotted their averages. Most land between fifty and sixty minutes, around the true value of fifty five. So we report a range, not one number. We say fifty five minutes, plus or minus five. A bigger sample shrinks the margin, but four times as many pupils only halves it. A big sample can still be wrong if it is not random. If we only ask pupils who stay after school, we miss those who leave early to work. Always ask who was left out. Quick check! Two random samples of forty pupils give fifty and sixty minutes. What is the best explanation? Random samples vary, so both answers are reasonable. Together they suggest the true value is somewhere near fifty five. A range tells that story honestly. In the app, open the sampling lab. Draw many samples, then make each sample bigger, and watch the averages crowd closer together. Your turn. We want a smaller margin of error. What should we do? Ask more pupils, chosen at random. Remember: samples wobble, so report a range, and check who your sample left out. Try it yourself: put numbered cards in a bag, draw ten at a time, and work out each average. Why are your averages all a little different?

body.en:
We rarely measure a whole population, so we estimate from a sample. A sample statistic, such as a sample mean, varies from sample to sample; its spread across repeated samples is the standard error, SE = s ÷ √n, where s is the sample standard deviation and n the sample size. An approximate 95% confidence interval is the estimate ± 2 SE. Because of the square root, quadrupling n only halves the SE.

Random error shrinks with n; bias does not. Selection bias arises when some groups are less likely to be sampled (an online survey misses people without internet), and non-response bias when some groups decline to answer. A huge biased sample gives a precise answer to the wrong question.

When you report, give the estimate, its interval and how the sample was drawn, and say who might be missing.
body.ar:
نادرًا ما نقيس مجتمعًا كاملًا، فنقدّر من عينة. وإحصاء العينة، كمتوسط العينة، يتغيّر من عينة إلى أخرى، وتشتّته عبر العينات المتكرّرة هو الخطأ المعياري، خ م = ع ÷ √ن، حيث ع الانحراف المعياري للعينة ون حجمها. وفترة ثقة تقريبية بنسبة ٩٥٪ هي التقدير ± ٢ خ م. وبسبب الجذر التربيعي، فإن مضاعفة ن أربع مرات تنصّف الخطأ المعياري فقط.

يصغر الخطأ العشوائي مع ن، أما التحيّز فلا. وينشأ تحيّز الاختيار حين تقلّ فرصة بعض المجموعات في الدخول إلى العينة (فالاستبيان الإلكتروني يفوّت من لا يملكون إنترنت)، وتحيّز عدم الاستجابة حين ترفض بعض المجموعات الإجابة. والعينة الضخمة المتحيّزة تعطي إجابة دقيقة عن السؤال الخطأ.

وحين تكتب تقريرك، اذكر التقدير وفترته وكيف سُحبت العينة، وقل من قد يكون غائبًا.

transcript.en: Our library log shows how often each pupil borrows and how long they keep each book. Nobody has sorted the pupils into types. Are there natural groups hiding in the data? Today: how a computer can find groups in data that nobody has labelled. Classification learns from examples that already have labels. Clustering has no labels at all. It looks for groups of cases that sit close together. First choose k, the number of groups, and drop k centres anywhere. Each pupil joins the nearest centre. Then each centre moves to the middle of its pupils, and we repeat until nothing moves. With k equal to three, the library pupils settled into three groups. Thirty pupils borrow often, forty borrow now and then, and twenty almost never. Moving a centre is just finding a mean. The new centre's position is the average of its pupils' loans and the average of their days kept. Careful with names. The computer only found pupils with similar numbers. Calling a group lazy readers is our story, not the data's, and it can follow a child around. Quick check! A group has three pupils who borrowed two, four and six books. Where does the centre move for loans? To four, the mean of two, four and six. The centre always moves to the middle of the pupils who joined it. That is the means in k-means. In the app, open the k-means lab. Press step and watch pupils change colour and centres move, then try a different k. Your turn. Does clustering need examples that already have labels? No, it finds groups on its own. Remember: choose k, join the nearest centre, move each centre to its mean, repeat, and name groups with care. Try it yourself: plot the sleep and screen time of a few friends, without names, and look for groups. Give each group a kind, neutral name.

body.en:
Clustering is unsupervised: there are no labels, and the goal is to find groups of similar observations. k-means chooses k centroids and alternates two steps: assign each point to its nearest centroid, then move each centroid to the mean of its points. Each round lowers the within-cluster sum of squared distances, so the algorithm converges, but only to a local optimum: different starting centroids can give different results, so run it several times.

Choosing k is a judgement. The elbow method plots the within-cluster error against k and looks for the point where adding clusters stops helping much. k-means also assumes roughly round clusters of similar size, and it is sensitive to feature scales and outliers.

A cluster is a pattern in the features you chose, not a natural kind. Naming clusters, such as “low-engagement users”, is an interpretation that can stigmatise real people.
body.ar:
التجميع غير موجَّه: لا توجد تسميات، والهدف إيجاد مجموعات من المشاهدات المتشابهة. وتختار k-means عددًا k من المراكز وتتناوب بين خطوتين: تعيين كل نقطة لأقرب مركز، ثم نقل كل مركز إلى متوسط نقاطه. وكل جولة تخفض مجموع مربّعات المسافات داخل العناقيد، فتتقارب الخوارزمية، لكن إلى حلّ أمثل محلي فقط: فقد تعطي مراكز بداية مختلفة نتائج مختلفة، فشغّلها مرات عدّة.

واختيار k حكم تقديري. فطريقة المرفق ترسم خطأ العناقيد مقابل k وتبحث عن النقطة التي تتوقف عندها إضافة العناقيد عن الإفادة كثيرًا. وتفترض k-means أيضًا عناقيد مستديرة تقريبًا ومتقاربة الحجم، وهي حسّاسة لمقاييس الخصائص والقيم الشاذة.

والعنقود نمط في الخصائص التي اخترتها، لا نوع طبيعي. وتسمية العناقيد، مثل «مستخدمون قليلو التفاعل»، تفسير قد يَصِم أناسًا حقيقيين.

steps.solution:
x = [1, 2, 3, 8, 9, 10]
c = [2, 5]
g = [[], []]
for v in x:
    k = 0 if abs(v - c[0]) <= abs(v - c[1]) else 1

transcript.en: We tried an app that listens to pupils read aloud and scores them. Overall it was right nine times in ten. But pupils from the village were marked down far more often. Today: how a model can be good on average and still unfair to some pupils. A model is biased when its mistakes fall more on one group than another. The average can look fine while one group carries most of the errors. So we check every group separately. Split the test pupils by group and work out the error rate for each one. If one group's rate is much higher, the model is not fair to them, whatever the overall score says. Here are the app's errors for each group of pupils. Town pupils had six wrong scores per hundred, while village pupils had twenty two. Most bias starts in the data. The app learned from recordings of town voices, so village accents were rare in its training. A model can only be as fair as the examples it learned from. We did three things. We stopped using the app's score for any decision, we sent the company recordings from our village pupils, and a teacher now listens whenever the app gives a low score. Quick check! The app is right ninety percent of the time overall. Does that show it is fair to every group of pupils? No. A good average can hide one group with many more errors. You only see bias when you check every group separately. In the app, open the bias lab. Change how many examples of each group are in the training data, and watch each group's error rate. Your turn. Where does most bias in a model start? In the data it learned from. Remember: averages hide unfairness, so compare errors group by group, fix the data, and keep a person in the loop. Try it yourself: try a voice assistant with different voices in your family, and count its mistakes for each person. Does it work equally well for everyone?

body.en:
A model can be accurate overall yet unfair to a group. Audit it by splitting the test results by group and comparing error rates: the false positive rate, FP ÷ (FP + TN), and the false negative rate, FN ÷ (FN + TP). In a speech-scoring app, if rural speakers get far more false “fail” results, the model harms them even if overall accuracy is high.

Bias usually starts in the data: some groups are under-represented, historic decisions encoded in labels were themselves unfair, or a feature acts as a proxy for a protected attribute, as a postcode can for ethnicity or income. Removing the protected attribute alone does not remove its proxies.

Fairness criteria can conflict. When base rates differ between groups, a model generally cannot equalise both its error rates and its calibration at once, so people must choose which kind of fairness matters for the decision, and keep a human review for high-stakes cases.
body.ar:
قد يكون النموذج دقيقًا إجمالًا ومع ذلك ظالمًا لمجموعة. فراجعه بتقسيم نتائج الاختبار حسب المجموعة ومقارنة نسب الخطأ: نسبة الإيجابيات الكاذبة، إ ك ÷ (إ ك + س ص)، ونسبة السلبيات الكاذبة، س ك ÷ (س ك + إ ص). ففي تطبيق لتقييم النطق، إذا نال المتحدّثون من الريف نتائج «رسوب» كاذبة أكثر بكثير، فالنموذج يضرّهم حتى لو كانت دقته الإجمالية عالية.

يبدأ التحيّز عادةً في البيانات: فبعض المجموعات ممثَّلة تمثيلًا ناقصًا، أو كانت القرارات التاريخية المرمّزة في التسميات نفسها ظالمة، أو تعمل خاصية بديلًا عن صفة محمية، كما قد يعمل الرمز البريدي بديلًا عن العِرق أو الدخل. وحذف الصفة المحمية وحده لا يحذف بدائلها.

وقد تتعارض معايير العدالة. فحين تختلف النسب الأساسية بين المجموعات، لا يستطيع النموذج عمومًا أن يساوي نسب أخطائه ومعايرته معًا، فيجب أن يختار الناس أيّ نوع من العدالة يهمّ للقرار، وأن يُبقوا مراجعة بشرية للحالات عالية المخاطر.

transcript.en: Our school wanted to move the start of the day later. Some said students would sleep more and learn better. Others worried about parents' work. How could data help decide? Today: how a school can use data to decide well, and when data is not enough. Data cannot make a decision for you. It shows what is likely to happen and to whom. People still weigh what matters most, and they own the decision. We wrote one clear question: if we start thirty minutes later, will lateness and tiredness fall? Then we chose what to measure before collecting anything, so we could not pick the numbers we liked afterwards. Two classes started later for six weeks while two similar classes did not. Late arrivals per week fell from twelve to five in the trial classes, and barely changed in the others. Numbers were only half the story. We also asked parents and pupils, and some families could not manage the later finish. Their voices changed our plan more than any chart. Ms Farah shared the results with everyone, including what did not work. Now any student can bring a question to the school's monthly data meeting. Small honest trials have become how the school decides. Quick check! Why did we keep two similar classes on the old start time during the trial? To compare fairly. Lateness might have fallen anyway, because of the weather or the season. The other classes show what would have happened without the change. In the app, open the decision lab. Weigh the evidence and the voices for a school change, and see how your choice affects each group. Your turn. The data shows a later start cuts lateness. Who should make the final decision? The school's people, using the data and the voices together. Remember: ask one clear question, run a fair trial, listen as well as count, and share what you find. Try it yourself: think of one change you would like at your school, and plan a small fair trial. Then present your plan to your class, with the data you would collect.
transcript.ar: مدرستنا كانت عايزة تأخر بداية اليوم الدراسي. ناس قالوا الطلاب هيناموا أكتر ويتعلموا أحسن. وناس قلقوا على شغل الأهالي. البيانات تقدر تساعد في القرار إزاي؟ النهارده: إزاي مدرسة تستعمل البيانات علشان تقرر صح، وإمتى البيانات متكفيش. البيانات مش هتقرر بدالك. هي بتبيّن إيه اللي غالبًا هيحصل ولمين. والناس برضه بيوزنوا إيه الأهم، وهم أصحاب القرار. كتبنا سؤال واحد واضح: لو بدأنا متأخرين نص ساعة، التأخير والتعب هيقلّوا؟ وبعدين اخترنا هنقيس إيه قبل ما نجمع أي حاجة، علشان منقدرش ننقّي الأرقام اللي عاجبانا بعدين. فصلين بدأوا متأخر لمدة ست أسابيع وفصلين شبههم لأ. التأخيرات في الأسبوع نزلت من اتناشر لخمسة في فصول التجربة، وتقريبًا ماتغيرتش في الباقيين. الأرقام كانت نص الحكاية بس. سألنا كمان الأهالي والتلاميذ، وبعض العيلات ماقدرتش على المواعيد المتأخرة في آخر اليوم. وأصواتهم غيّرت خطتنا أكتر من أي رسم. الأستاذة فرح شاركت النتايج مع الكل، ومعاها اللي ماشتغلش. ودلوقتي أي طالب يقدر يجيب سؤال لاجتماع البيانات الشهري في المدرسة. والتجارب الصغيرة الأمينة بقت طريقة المدرسة في القرار. سؤال سريع! ليه خلّينا فصلين شبههم على الميعاد القديم وقت التجربة؟ علشان نقارن بعدل. التأخير كان ممكن يقل كده كده، بسبب الجو أو الموسم. والفصول التانية بتبيّن كان هيحصل إيه من غير التغيير. في التطبيق، افتح معمل القرار. وازن الأدلة والأصوات لتغيير في المدرسة، وشوف اختيارك بيأثر إزاي على كل مجموعة. دورك. البيانات بتبيّن إن البداية المتأخرة بتقلل التأخير. مين المفروض ياخد القرار النهائي؟ ناس المدرسة، وهم بيستعملوا البيانات والأصوات مع بعض. افتكر: اسأل سؤال واحد واضح، واعمل تجربة عادلة، واسمع كمان مش بس عدّ، وشارك اللي لقيته. جرّبها بنفسك: فكّر في تغيير واحد نفسك فيه في مدرستك، وخطط لتجربة صغيرة عادلة. وبعدين اعرض خطتك على فصلك، مع البيانات اللي هتجمعها.

prompt.en: Read

body.en:
Observational data shows associations, but confounders, variables that affect both the treatment and the outcome, can create or hide effects. Schools that start later may also differ in funding or location. The strongest design is a randomised controlled trial: randomly assign units to treatment or control, so confounders balance out on average.

When randomisation is impossible, difference-in-differences compares the change in a treated group with the change in a similar untreated group over the same period: effect = (treated after − before) − (control after − before). It assumes both groups would have followed parallel trends without the treatment.

Good decisions also need a pre-registered question and measures, so results cannot be cherry-picked; consent and privacy for participants; and the voices of the people affected, since some costs never appear in the numbers. Data informs a decision; accountable people make it.
body.ar:
تُظهر البيانات الرصدية ارتباطات، لكن المتغيّرات المربكة، وهي متغيّرات تؤثّر في المعالجة والنتيجة معًا، قد تصنع آثارًا أو تخفيها. فالمدارس التي تبدأ متأخرة قد تختلف أيضًا في التمويل أو الموقع. وأقوى تصميم هو التجربة العشوائية المضبوطة: وزّع الوحدات عشوائيًا على المعالجة أو الضبط، فتتوازن المتغيّرات المربكة في المتوسط.

وحين تتعذّر العشوائية، يقارن أسلوب الفرق في الفروق التغيّرَ في مجموعة معالَجة بالتغيّر في مجموعة مشابهة غير معالَجة خلال الفترة نفسها: الأثر = (المعالَجة بعد − قبل) − (الضبط بعد − قبل). ويفترض أن المجموعتين كانتا ستتّبعان اتجاهات متوازية لولا المعالجة.

وتحتاج القرارات الجيدة أيضًا إلى سؤال ومقاييس مسجّلة مسبقًا، حتى لا تُنتقى النتائج، وإلى موافقة المشاركين وخصوصيتهم، وإلى أصوات المتأثّرين، لأن بعض التكاليف لا تظهر في الأرقام أبدًا. فالبيانات توضّح القرار، والأشخاص المسؤولون يتّخذونه.

steps.solution:
t_before, t_after = 12, 5
c_before, c_after = 11, 10
effect = (t_after - t_before) - (c_after - c_before)
print(effect)
